Avoid application to chest/areas of infant contact

summary: Hydroquinone is a topical skin-lightening agent used to fade hyperpigmentation such as melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, freckles and age spots. It inhibits melanin formation in melanocytes. OTC products contain ~2% and prescription-strength products ~4%; it is applied as a thin layer once or twice daily, usually with sun protection. Long-term or high-strength use can cause exogenous ochronosis and irritation.
indications: Gradual fading of hyperpigmented skin (age spots, freckles, lentigines)
Melasma / chloasma and other forms of melanin hyperpigmentation

dosage.d: Apply a thin layer to the affected area once or twice daily
dosage.n: Use sunscreen during the day; test on a small area first

dosage.d: Apply a thin layer to the hyperpigmented area twice daily
dosage.n: Reassess at ~3 months; discontinue if no improvement

dosage.d: Not recommended except under physician supervision

admin: Apply only to the affected (hyperpigmented) area, avoiding surrounding normal skin
Wash and dry skin before applying a thin layer
Avoid contact with eyes, lips and mucous membranes
Apply broad-spectrum sunscreen and use protective clothing during the day
Do a small test-patch application before first full use to check for irritation
moa: Hydroquinone inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme required to convert tyrosine to melanin within melanocytes. By suppressing melanin synthesis and causing reversible inhibition of melanocyte metabolic processes, it reduces pigment production and gradually lightens hyperpigmented skin.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to hydroquinone or any formulation component
relative: Use on broken, sunburnt or irritated skin
monitor: Blue-black discoloration (exogenous ochronosis) with prolonged use

preg: Avoid in pregnancy. Systemic absorption can be substantial (roughly 25-35% of an applied dose) and human safety data are lacking; use only if clearly necessary after weighing benefit and risk.
lact: Avoid application to the chest or areas where the infant may have skin contact. The amount entering breast milk is unknown; limit use during breastfeeding.
renal: No dose adjustment needed; systemic absorption from topical use is low and effects are largely local.
hepatic: No dose adjustment needed; systemic exposure from topical application is minimal.

moderate: Peroxide products (benzoyl peroxide, hydrogen peroxide) - may cause temporary skin staining if used together
minor: Other topical irritants (retinoids, exfoliants) - additive irritation

serious: Exogenous ochronosis (blue-black skin discoloration) with prolonged use
emergency: Severe hypersensitivity reaction (marked swelling, blistering, difficulty breathing)

monitoring: Skin response to therapy and degree of lightening
Signs of ochronosis with prolonged or high-strength use
counsel: Apply only to dark patches, not the whole face, and use a thin layer
Always use sunscreen - sun exposure reverses the benefit and can worsen pigmentation
Stop and contact a doctor if marked irritation, blistering or blue-black discoloration develops
Improvement is gradual and may take several weeks; do not over-apply
Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding unless advised by a doctor
pk: Visible lightening usually over several weeks
Maximal effect after weeks to a few months of use
Not clinically defined for topical use
Effect reverses with sun exposure / on stopping
Store at room temperature; some products require refrigeration - follow label
pearls: Sold OTC (2%) and as prescription (4%) topical products; restricted/withdrawn as an OTC monograph drug in some regions - this record uses product label and standard dermatology references
Mandatory daily sunscreen - UV exposure stimulates melanin and undoes treatment
Limit duration and strength to reduce risk of exogenous ochronosis
Often combined with a retinoid and a topical steroid (triple combination) for melasma
missed: If a dose is missed, apply it when remembered, or skip it and resume the usual schedule. Do not apply extra product to make up a missed application.
overdose: Topical overdose may cause marked local irritation and burning. Accidental ingestion can cause nausea and, theoretically, methemoglobinemia and CNS effects with very large amounts - seek medical help. Treat skin overexposure by washing the area; manage ingestion with supportive care.
